title: Curvature changes everything
sub: Three optimizers on the Rosenbrock function, from the same start.

frames.caption: The Rosenbrock function: a long, curved, nearly flat valley (grey level sets) leading to the minimum at (1, 1). Everyone starts at the classic point (−1.2, 1). Gradient descent (orange) needs a small step to stay stable across the steep valley walls, so it crawls along the floor.

Newton's method (blue) solves H δ = −∇f at every step, jumping to the bottom of the local quadratic model. Far from the minimum the quadratic model is poor: its second step shoots far below the chart, to y ≈ −3.2. But the next step lands back in the valley, and from there it reaches (1, 1) in 6 steps in total.

BFGS (aqua) never computes the Hessian. It builds an approximation from the gradient changes it observes, with a line search to keep each step safe. It needs more steps than Newton (36) but each is as cheap as a gradient step, which is why L-BFGS is the workhorse for smooth problems.
Distance to the minimum, on a log scale, for the first 40 steps. Gradient descent (orange) barely moves: after 40 steps it is still 1.97 away, and it needs 11,379 steps to get within 0.001.

Newton: once it is close, the error is roughly squared at every step, so the number of correct digits about doubles: 0.06, then 10⁻⁵, 10⁻¹¹, then machine precision. That plunge is quadratic convergence. Far from the minimum there is no such guarantee, and pure Newton can even head for a saddle point or a maximum, which is why practical versions add a line search or trust region.
BFGS sits in between: superlinear convergence, without ever forming or inverting a Hessian.
